+"""Free source-only collection in an isolated root; never calls LLM or publication stages."""
+from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
+from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
+from pathlib import Path
+from collections import Counter
+import hashlib
+import json
+import os
+import subprocess
+import sys
+import time
+import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
+import requests
+import yaml
+
+REPO = Path.cwd()
+sys.path.insert(0, str(REPO))
+from scripts.feed import fetch_arxiv, fetch_hf, fetch_rss, fetch_s2, fetch_github
+from scripts.feed.health import update_health
+from scripts.feed.storage import save_raw, write_json, load_state
+
+ROOT = REPO / 'build/maintenance-2026-11-23/source-intake'
+REPORTS = ROOT / 'reports'
+REPORTS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+NOW = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
+DAY = '2026-11-23'
+assert NOW.date().isoformat() == DAY, 'Run date must match the intended daily source window.'
+START = json.loads((ROOT/'run-state.json').read_text())['started_at'] if (ROOT/'run-state.json').exists() else NOW.isoformat()
+REGISTRY = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / 'feed/sources.yaml').read_text())
+SOURCES = [s for s in REGISTRY['sources'] if s['enabled']]
+BASELINE = json.loads((ROOT / 'canonical-baseline.json').read_text())
+KNOWN = set(BASELINE['ids'])
+
+# Keep credential values inside their existing environment / gh client.
+# No local credential file is read and no model credential is loaded.
+environment_s2_present = bool(os.environ.get('S2_API_KEY', '').strip())
+gh_auth = subprocess.run(['gh','auth','status','--active'],capture_output=True,text=True)
+if os.environ.get('S2_API_KEY'):
+    os.environ['S2_API_KEY'] = os.environ['S2_API_KEY'].strip()
+AUTH = {'semantic_scholar': 'authenticated' if os.environ.get('S2_API_KEY') else 'anonymous',
+        'semantic_scholar_interval_seconds': 1.1 if os.environ.get('S2_API_KEY') else 3.1,
+        'semantic_scholar_max_429_retries': 5,
+        'github': 'authenticated_via_gh_cli' if gh_auth.returncode==0 else 'gh_cli_auth_unavailable',
+        'model_credentials_loaded': False}
+
+def relative(path):
+    return Path(path).relative_to(REPO).as_posix()
+
+def stamp():
+    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
+
+def sha(path):
+    return hashlib.sha256(Path(path).read_bytes()).hexdigest()
+
+class RecordingSession:
+    last_s2_dispatch_ns = None
+
+    def __init__(self, source_id):
+        self.session = requests.Session()
+        self.source_id = source_id
+        self.started = time.monotonic()
+        self.directory = ROOT / 'network' / source_id
+        self.directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+        self.attempts = []
+        self.path = self.directory / 'attempts.jsonl'
+
+    def get(self, url, **kwargs):
+        is_s2 = self.source_id.startswith('s2-')
+        previous_dispatch = RecordingSession.last_s2_dispatch_ns
+        if is_s2:
+            self.bounded_sleep(0)
+            if previous_dispatch is not None:
+                interval_ns = int(AUTH['semantic_scholar_interval_seconds'] * 1_000_000_000)
+                while time.monotonic_ns() < previous_dispatch + interval_ns:
+                    self.bounded_sleep((previous_dispatch + interval_ns - time.monotonic_ns()) / 1_000_000_000)
+            kwargs['timeout'] = min(kwargs.get('timeout', 30), self.remaining())
+        begin = time.monotonic()
+        row = {'requested_at': stamp(), 'request_url': url, 'params': kwargs.get('params'), 'status': 'started'}
+        try:
+            dispatch_ns = time.monotonic_ns()
+            row['dispatch_monotonic_ns'] = dispatch_ns
+            if is_s2:
+                row['previous_s2_dispatch_monotonic_ns'] = previous_dispatch
+                row['s2_dispatch_gap_seconds'] = (dispatch_ns - previous_dispatch) / 1_000_000_000 if previous_dispatch is not None else None
+                row['required_dispatch_gap_seconds'] = AUTH['semantic_scholar_interval_seconds']
+                RecordingSession.last_s2_dispatch_ns = dispatch_ns
+            if self.source_id == 'github-releases':
+                from urllib.parse import urlencode
+                endpoint=url.removeprefix('https://api.github.com/')
+                if kwargs.get('params'):endpoint+='?'+urlencode(kwargs['params'])
+                result=subprocess.run(['gh','api',endpoint,'--include'],capture_output=True,timeout=35)
+                if result.returncode and not result.stdout.startswith(b'HTTP/'):
+                    raise requests.ConnectionError('gh API request failed: '+result.stderr.decode(errors='replace').strip())
+                header,sep,content=result.stdout.replace(b'\r\n',b'\n').partition(b'\n\n')
+                if not sep:raise ValueError('GitHub response has no HTTP header boundary')
+                lines=header.decode().splitlines();response=requests.Response()
+                response.status_code=int(lines[0].split()[1]);response.url=url
+                response.headers.update(dict(line.split(': ',1) for line in lines[1:] if ': ' in line))
+                response._content=content
+            else:
+                response = self.session.get(url, **kwargs)
+            body = self.directory / f'{len(self.attempts)+1:04d}.body'
+            body.write_bytes(response.content)
+            row.update(http_status=response.status_code, final_url=response.url,
+                       status='http_response', body_path=relative(body), body_sha256=sha(body),
+                       bytes=len(response.content), content_type=response.headers.get('Content-Type'),
+                       http_date=response.headers.get('Date'),
+                       api_key_header_present=bool(kwargs.get('headers', {}).get('x-api-key')))
+            return response
+        except requests.RequestException as error:
+            row.update(status='network_error', error=f'{type(error).__name__}: {error}')
+            raise
+        finally:
+            row.update(finished_at=stamp(), elapsed_seconds=round(time.monotonic()-begin, 3))
+            self.attempts.append(row)
+            with self.path.open('a') as handle:
+                handle.write(json.dumps(row, ensure_ascii=False)+'\n')
+
+    def remaining(self):
+        value = 180 - (time.monotonic() - self.started)
+        if value <= 0:
+            raise ValueError('BoundedSourceTraversal: source reached the 180-second attempt window; successful responses retained; unvisited coverage is unknown.')
+        return value
+
+    def bounded_sleep(self, seconds):
+        remaining = self.remaining()
+        if seconds >= remaining:
+            time.sleep(remaining)
+            self.remaining()
+        if seconds > 0:
+            time.sleep(seconds)
+
+
+def bounded_s2_request(path, params=None, session=None):
+    """Bound retries and pacing at the actual recorded transport boundary."""
+    assert isinstance(session, RecordingSession)
+    headers = {'User-Agent': 'FollowRSI/0.1'}
+    if os.environ.get('S2_API_KEY'):
+        headers['x-api-key'] = os.environ['S2_API_KEY']
+    for attempt in range(6):
+        response = session.get(fetch_s2.BASE + '/' + path, params=params, headers=headers, timeout=30)
+        if response.status_code != 429 or attempt == 5:
+            response.raise_for_status()
+            return response.json()
+        session.bounded_sleep(AUTH['semantic_scholar_interval_seconds'] * 2 ** attempt)
+
+
+fetch_s2.request = bounded_s2_request
+
+write_json(ROOT/'auth-presence.json', {'checked_at': stamp(), 'environment_s2_key_present': environment_s2_present, 'env_local_s2_key_present': 'not_read', 'run_mode': AUTH['semantic_scholar'], 'collector_explicitly_clears_s2_key': False, 'configured_key_was_skipped': 'unknown_local_secret_file_not_read', 'credentials_printed': False, 'model_credentials_loaded': False})
+write_json(ROOT/'run-state.json', {'status':'running','started_at':START,'target_day':DAY,'auth':AUTH,'enabled_sources':[s['id'] for s in SOURCES], 'paid_calls':0, 'production_writes':0})
+
+ERRORS = (requests.RequestException, ET.ParseError, ValueError, KeyError, TypeError)
+
+def collect(source):
+    source_id = source['id']
+    checkpoint = ROOT/'source-results'/f'{source_id}.json'
+    if checkpoint.exists():
+        saved=json.loads(checkpoint.read_text())
+        return saved
+    begin=time.monotonic();started=stamp();session=RecordingSession(source_id)
+    print(json.dumps({'event':'source_started','source':source_id,'at':started}),flush=True)
+    found=[];raw=None;degraded=False;failure=None;api_failure=None
+    try:
+        kind=source['kind']
+        if kind=='hf_daily':
+            full_board_source = {**source, 'params': {**source['params'], 'keywords': []}}
+            found,raw=fetch_hf.fetch(full_board_source,now=NOW,session=session,days=6)
+            # A Monday request can be three days beyond the most recent open list.
+            limits = sorted({a['available_through'] for a in raw['attempts'].values() if a.get('available_through')})
+            latest = limits[-1] if limits else None
+            if latest and latest not in raw['attempts']:
+                latest_now = datetime.fromisoformat(latest + 'T00:00:00+00:00')
+                more, extra = fetch_hf.fetch(full_board_source,now=latest_now,session=session,days=1)
+                found.extend(more)
+                for key in ['days','attempts','errors']:
+                    raw[key].update(extra[key])
+            raw['most_recent_explicit_available_day'] = latest
+            raw['coverage_note'] = 'All members from each successful requested board are retained in raw responses; reconciliation disables the keyword prefilter.'
+        elif kind=='arxiv_query':
+            try:
+                found,raw=fetch_arxiv.fetch(source,days=6,now=NOW,session=session)
+            except ERRORS as error:
+                failures=load_state(ROOT)['sources'].get(source_id,{}).get('consecutive_errors',0)
+                if failures<2:
+                    raise
+                api_failure=f'{type(error).__name__}: {error}'
+                found,raw=fetch_arxiv.fallback_rss(source,now=NOW.isoformat(),session=session)
+                raw['api_error']=api_failure;degraded=True
+        elif kind in {'s2_citations','s2_authors'}:
+            found,raw=fetch_s2.fetch(source,ROOT,now=NOW,session=session)
+        elif kind=='rss':
+            found,raw=fetch_rss.fetch(source,now=NOW,session=session)
+        elif kind=='github_releases':
+            found,raw=fetch_github.fetch(source,ROOT,now=NOW,session=session)
+        else:
+            raise ValueError('Unsupported enabled source kind: '+kind)
+    except ERRORS as error:
+        failure=f'{type(error).__name__}: {error}'
+    recovered_pages=[]
+    if source['kind'] in {'s2_citations','s2_authors'} and failure:
+        # A later 429 must not discard pages which have already returned HTTP 200.
+        seed_ids={p['arxiv']:p['id'] for p in fetch_s2.seed_papers(yaml.safe_load((ROOT/'data/papers.yaml').read_text())['papers'])}
+        seen_pages=set();retained_metadata=[]
+        for receipt in session.attempts:
+            if receipt.get('http_status')!=200:
+                continue
+            payload=json.loads((REPO/receipt['body_path']).read_text())
+            url=receipt['request_url'];params=receipt.get('params') or {}
+            retained_metadata.append({'request_url':url,'params':params,'body_path':receipt['body_path'],'body_sha256':receipt['body_sha256']})
+            if not (url.endswith('/citations') or url.endswith('/papers')):
+                continue
+            key=(url,params.get('offset'))
+            if key in seen_pages:
+                continue
+            seen_pages.add(key)
+            seed=seed_ids.get(url.split('paper/arXiv:',1)[1].removesuffix('/citations')) if '/citations' in url else None
+            parsed=fetch_s2.parse_json(payload,source_id,seed_id=seed,author_tracked=source['kind']=='s2_authors',now=NOW.isoformat())
+            cutoff=(NOW-timedelta(days=30)).date().isoformat()
+            found.extend(x for x in parsed if x['published'] and x['published']>=cutoff)
+            recovered_pages.append({**retained_metadata[-1],'unfiltered_records':len(parsed)})
+        raw={'format':'s2-partial-recovery-from-network-receipts','auth_mode':AUTH['semantic_scholar'],'source_failed':True,
+             'failure':failure,'pages':recovered_pages,'successful_http_responses':retained_metadata,
+             'records':found,'coverage_note':'Only successful responses recovered; source traversal ended early.'}
+    observed_at=stamp()
+    for record in found:
+        record['source_observed_at']=observed_at
+        record['first_seen']=observed_at
+        record['first_seen_policy']='actual_source_collection_timestamp'
+    raw_path=None
+    if raw is not None:
+        raw_path=save_raw(ROOT,source_id,DAY,raw)
+    if raw and raw.get('errors'):
+        failure=str(raw['errors'])
+    outcome={'source_id':source_id,'kind':source['kind'],'started_at':started,'finished_at':stamp(),
+             'elapsed_seconds':round(time.monotonic()-begin,3),'ok':failure is None,'count':len(found),
+             'unique_ids':len({x['id'] for x in found}),'ids':[x['id'] for x in found],
+             'degraded':degraded,'error':failure or api_failure,'api_error_before_fallback':api_failure,
+             'request_count':len(session.attempts),'http_status_counts':dict(Counter(str(x.get('http_status',x['status'])) for x in session.attempts)),
+             'network_attempts':relative(session.path),'raw_path':relative(raw_path) if raw_path else None,
+             'records':found,'raw_available':raw is not None}
+    if source_id.startswith('s2-'):
+        outcome['auth_mode']=AUTH['semantic_scholar'];outcome['min_interval_seconds']=AUTH['semantic_scholar_interval_seconds']
+        outcome.update(recovered_partial=bool(recovered_pages),recovered_successful_pages=len(recovered_pages),source_traversal_complete=failure is None)
+    if source_id=='hf-daily' and raw:
+        payload=raw.get('days',{}).get(DAY)
+        attempt=raw.get('attempts',{}).get(DAY,{})
+        outcome['hf_today']={'date':DAY,'request_status':attempt.get('status'),'available_through':attempt.get('available_through'),
+                            'raw_members':len(payload) if payload is not None else None,
+                            'all_requested_board_records':len(found), 'keyword_prefilter_enabled':False,
+                            'paper_ids':[x['paper']['id'] for x in payload] if payload is not None else [],
+                            'all_requested_board_ids':[x['id'] for x in found],
+                            'date_meaning':'Membership in the explicitly requested HF daily recommendation list; not paper publication or first_seen.',
+                            'original_dates_verified':False,'qualified_harness_count':None}
+    write_json(checkpoint,outcome)
+    print(json.dumps({'event':'source_completed','source':source_id,'at':outcome['finished_at'],'ok':outcome['ok'],'count':len(found),'requests':len(session.attempts),'degraded':degraded},ensure_ascii=False),flush=True)
+    return outcome
+
+# HF first. Each API family remains serial so rate-limit guarantees are preserved.
+outcomes=[]
+for source in SOURCES:
+    if source['kind']=='hf_daily':
+        outcomes.append(collect(source))
+groups=[ [s for s in SOURCES if s['kind']=='arxiv_query'],
+         [s for s in SOURCES if s['kind'] in {'s2_citations','s2_authors'}],
+         [s for s in SOURCES if s['kind']=='rss'],
+         [s for s in SOURCES if s['kind']=='github_releases'] ]
+def collect_group(group):
+    return [collect(s) for s in group]
+with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
+    pending=[pool.submit(collect_group,g) for g in groups if g]
+    for completed in as_completed(pending):
+        outcomes.extend(completed.result())
+
+
+write_json(ROOT/'run-state.json',{'status':'source_collection_complete','target_day':DAY,'started_at':START,'finished_at':stamp(),'paid_calls':0,'production_writes':0,'auth':AUTH,'completed_sources':[x['source_id'] for x in outcomes]})
+print(json.dumps({'event':'all_sources_complete','sources':len(outcomes),'records':sum(x['count'] for x in outcomes)},ensure_ascii=False),flush=True)

+    <title>cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-20T06:26:11Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27193v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27193v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.</summary>

+    <title>NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-20T11:47:47Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27499v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27499v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.</summary>

+    <title>Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming</title>

+    <summary>It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp</summary>

+    <title>MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-20T18:51:29Z</updated>

+    <summary>Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.</summary>

+    <title>Generalist Action Critic: Harnessing Frontier Models in Autonomous Driving</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-20T16:32:53Z</updated>

+    <summary>Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.</summary>

+    <summary>Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis shows that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.</summary>

+    <title>PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-19T18:59:34Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26624v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

+    <summary>Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.</summary>

+    <summary>We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. +    <summary>Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.</summary>

+    <summary>Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.</summary>

+    <summary>Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.</summary>

+    <summary>As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.</summary>

+    <title>CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-20T04:40:59Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27116v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

+    <summary>The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.</summary>

+    <updated>2026-11-19T20:48:58Z</updated>

+    <summary>Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.</summary>

+    <summary>Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.</summary>

+    <summary>Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.</summary>

+    <title>One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-19T18:58:14Z</updated>

+    <summary>Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.</summary>

+    <summary>Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.</summary>

+    <summary>Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.</summary>

+    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.</summary>

+    <summary>Prompt enhancement (PE) refines concise user prompts into detailed descriptions to improve the compositional aesthetics of generated images while preserving user intent. A common practice constructs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pairs by deriving short, user-like prompts from dense captions, implicitly assuming that captions that improve image generation also provide effective supervision. In this paper, however, we uncover a counterintuitive finding: PE models trained on caption pairs with substantial generation gains perform comparably to those trained on pairs with only marginal gains. We argue that dense captions can impose redundant supervision by requiring PE models to reproduce image-specific details weakly related to user intent. Motivated by this discrepancy, we introduce Prune to Expand (P2E), a simple text-only method that refines dense-caption supervision by selectively removing redundant sentences under a per-example deletion bound while preserving explicit user requirements and informative visual structure. Extensive experiments under identical training configurations demonstrate that P2E improves alignment with human preferences and visual quality over conventional dense-caption SFT across diverse image categories and visual generators.</summary>

+    <summary>Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and evaluation. +    <summary>Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. +    <title>Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-19T18:46:50Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26590v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

+    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.</summary>

+    <summary>Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.</summary>

+    <summary>Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.</summary>

+    <summary>We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .</summary>

+    <title>Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-20T16:09:46Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27780v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

+    <summary>Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.</summary>

+    <summary>Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.</summary>

+    <summary>Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.</summary>

+    <summary>Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. +    <summary>Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).</summary>

+    <updated>2026-11-19T17:15:38Z</updated>

+    <summary>Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. +    <summary>Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.</summary>

+    <summary>Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.</summary>

+    <title>Learning In-Context Adaptivity for LLMs through Continual Gameplay</title>
+    <updated>2026-11-16T18:58:49Z</updated>

+    <summary>LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks where they must explore, gather experience, and adapt their decisions accordingly. We name this capability in-context adaptivity: improving decisions across episodes from experience accumulated in context. We propose to evaluate it in repeated imperfect-information games against unknown opponents. In these games, fixed game-theoretically optimal policies cannot achieve maximum reward, whereas adapting to the opponent increases returns across games. We design a paired protocol that evaluates each agent with and without memory under identical conditions to isolate experience gain from single-game skill. Evaluation shows that memory brings little performance gain for open-weight models and inconsistent gains for frontier models. Our analysis of the agents' summaries and actions identifies a memory-doing gap in which models accurately record opponent tendencies yet rarely depart from default play. To close this gap, we construct a pool of exploitable opponents and post-train Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. We optimize full-match return across context segments so summary generation and action selection are trained together. On unseen opponents, our 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over supervised fine-tuning in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em. Across 35 opponents, our policy matches or surpasses frontier models, generalizes beyond its training horizon, and retains most of its gain on summaries from frontier models.</summary>

+    <title>When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments</title>

+    <summary>Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.</summary>

+    <summary>Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. +    <summary>Audio artificial intelligence (AI) now recognizes speech, sounds, and music remarkably well, yet voice agents still act when they should not: they execute commands addressed to others, act on misheard content, and commit before the user finishes speaking. This position article argues that the bottleneck in agentic audio AI has shifted from recognition to decision-making. We propose a reference architecture with an explicit decision layer, separate from perception and reasoning, that chooses whether to act, wait, ask, or remain silent from evidence on addressedness, speaker identity, content confidence, tool reliability, utterance completeness, and action risk. We motivate the design through six recurring decision failures and a decision-theoretic argument that transcript confidence alone is insufficient to justify an action. We implement the layer with fuzzy inference, evolutionary optimization, and sequential decision-making, and evaluate it through simulations, ablations, and recorded audio, including egocentric recordings. Addressedness and speaker evidence matter most, risk-aware gating suppresses costly errors, and well-tuned policies perform similarly, with fuzzy gates more robust to overconfident addressedness estimates. On recorded audio, explicit gating cuts executed side talk from 41\% to 7--10\% while serving 83--85\% of valid requests under successful clarification, outperforming prompting-based baselines. These results support explicit action gating as an architectural requirement for reliable voice agents.</summary>

+    <summary>Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. +    <summary>Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. +    <summary>Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.</summary>

+    <summary>Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. +    <summary>Long-horizon visual agents must do more than inspect images: they must turn observations into evidence that remains usable as a task unfolds. Existing active-perception methods teach agents where and how to look, while a final-answer reward gives little structure for deciding which observations satisfy dependent subgoals or should be retained for later use. We present ViStep-RL (Visual Stepwise Reinforcement Learning), which models execution as a dependency-linked graph of evidence-bearing subgoals. A verifier tracks which subgoals are supported by valid evidence, and changes in graph potential provide a net-progress learning signal; an active memory protocol preserves evidence across turns and links retrieval to downstream use. On ViInteract, ViStep-RL reaches 60.0% strict completion with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, compared with 10.0% for the base model and 46.5% after supervised fine-tuning. Controlled studies show that incremental task-state rewards outperform cumulative rewards by 3.2 points, while active evidence writing improves strict completion by 7.75 points over automatic writing. Under a common interaction framework, the task-trained ViStep-RL policy achieves 59.5% answer accuracy, 24.0 points above the strongest of six general-purpose reference models. Held-out episodes confirm the gain at both Qwen scales, and gains extend to three external visual reasoning benchmarks.</summary>

+    <summary>Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.</summary>

+    <title>Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading</title>

+    <summary>Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.</summary>
