+    <summary>LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.</summary>

+    <summary>Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? +    <summary>Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. +  Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. +    <summary>An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. +    <summary>Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. +    <summary>Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. +    <summary>Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.</summary>

+    <summary>Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.</summary>

+    <summary>Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. +    <summary>3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. +    <summary>Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. +    <summary>Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.</summary>

+    <summary>Given an image and successive user instructions, sequential image editing should return an updated image that satisfies each new request and preserves earlier requirements that remain active. +      "abstract": "Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.",

+      "abstract": "Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. +      "title": "Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception",
+      "abstract": "LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.",

+      "abstract": "Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\\%$ to $86.9\\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. +      "abstract": "An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. +      "abstract": "Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. +      "abstract": "Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. +      "abstract": "Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. +      "abstract": "3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. +WORK = ROOT / 'build/maintenance-2026-11-23/source-intake'

+
+
+def save(name, value):
+    (WORK / name).write_text(json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) + '\n')
+
+
+def sha(path):
+    return hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
+
+
+base = {x['id']: x for x in map(json.loads, (WORK / 'canonical-baseline.jsonl').read_text().splitlines())}
+prior_observations = {}
+watch_path = WORK.parent / 'pr-audit/issue-canonical-mapping.json'
+if watch_path.exists():
+    for issue in json.loads(watch_path.read_text()):
+        for aid in issue['arxiv_ids']:
+            ident = 'arxiv:' + aid
+            known = prior_observations.get(ident)
+            if not known or issue['created_at'] < known['observed_at']:
+                prior_observations[ident] = {'observed_at': issue['created_at'],
+                    'source': 'repository arxiv-watch issue', 'url': issue['url'],
+                    'evidence_path': str(watch_path.relative_to(ROOT)), 'evidence_sha256': sha(watch_path)}
+
+
+def first_seen(ident, collected_at):
+    if ident in base:
+        return base[ident]['first_seen']
+    prior = prior_observations.get(ident)
+    return min(prior['observed_at'], collected_at) if prior else collected_at
+
+sources = [x for x in yaml.safe_load((WORK / 'feed/sources.yaml').read_text())['sources'] if x['enabled']]
+seed_ids = {x['arxiv']: x['id'] for x in fetch_s2.seed_papers(yaml.safe_load((WORK / 'data/papers.yaml').read_text())['papers'])}
+official = {}
+for path in [WORK / 'official-metadata/records.json', WORK / 'official-metadata/extra/records.json']:
+    if path.exists():
+        official.update({x['arxiv_id']: x for x in json.loads(path.read_text())['records']})
+raw_rows, eligible, receipts_by_source, source_summaries = [], [], {}, []
+observed = {}
+for source in sources:
+    sid, kind = source['id'], source['kind']
+    checkpoint = WORK / 'source-results' / f'{sid}.json'
+    result = json.loads(checkpoint.read_text()) if checkpoint.exists() else None
+    receipt_path = WORK / 'network' / sid / 'attempts.jsonl'
+    receipts = [json.loads(x) for x in receipt_path.read_text().splitlines()] if receipt_path.exists() else []
+    receipts_by_source[sid] = receipts
+    source_raw, source_eligible = [], []
+    dispositions = Counter()
+    for receipt in receipts:
+        if receipt.get('http_status') != 200:
+            continue
+        path = ROOT / receipt['body_path']
+        assert sha(path) == receipt['body_sha256'], path
+        now, url = receipt['requested_at'], receipt['request_url']
+        if kind == 'hf_daily':
+            records = fetch_hf.parse_json(json.loads(path.read_text()), sid, keywords=[], now=now,
+                                         daily_date=receipt['params']['date'])
+        elif kind == 'arxiv_query':
+            if url.startswith('https://rss.arxiv.org/'):
+                records = fetch_rss.parse_feed(path.read_bytes(), sid, now=now, feed_url=receipt['final_url'])
+            else:
+                records = fetch_arxiv.parse_atom(path.read_text(), sid, now=now)
+        elif kind == 'rss':
+            records = fetch_rss.parse_feed(path.read_bytes(), sid, now=now, feed_url=receipt['final_url'])
+        elif kind == 'github_releases':
+            repository = url.split('/repos/', 1)[1].removesuffix('/releases')
+            records = fetch_github.parse_json(json.loads(path.read_text()), repository, sid, now=now)
+        elif url.endswith(('/citations', '/papers')):
+            seed_id = seed_ids.get(url.split('paper/arXiv:', 1)[1].removesuffix('/citations')) if '/citations' in url else None
+            records = fetch_s2.parse_json(json.loads(path.read_text()), sid,
+                                         seed_id=seed_id,
+                                         author_tracked=kind == 's2_authors', now=now)
+        else:
+            # S2 seed author metadata is coverage evidence, not a discovered paper page.
+            continue
+        for index, record in enumerate(records):
+            ident = record['id']
+            observed[ident] = min(observed.get(ident, now), now)
+            record['source_observed_at'] = now
+            record['first_seen'] = first_seen(ident, now)
+            record['first_seen_policy'] = 'preserve_canonical' if ident in base else 'earliest_verified_repository_observation' if ident in prior_observations else 'actual_source_observation'
+            if ident in prior_observations and ident not in base:
+                record['first_seen_evidence'] = prior_observations[ident]
+            date = str(record.get('source_published') or record['published'])[:10]
+            if kind in {'hf_daily', 'arxiv_query'}:
+                disposition = 'within_requested_source_window'
+            elif kind in {'s2_citations', 's2_authors'}:
+                cutoff = (NOW - timedelta(days=30)).date().isoformat()
+                disposition = ('missing_publication_date' if not date else 'before_source_window' if date < cutoff
+                               else 'after_target_date' if date > DAY else 'within_requested_source_window')
+            else:
+                cutoff = (NOW - timedelta(days=source['params'].get('lookback_days', 14) - 1)).date().isoformat()
+                disposition = ('needs_official_metadata' if not date and record.get('arxiv_id')
+                               else 'missing_publication_date' if not date else 'before_source_window' if date < cutoff
+                               else 'after_target_date' if date > DAY else 'within_requested_source_window')
+            evidence = {key: receipt[key] for key in ('requested_at', 'finished_at', 'request_url', 'body_path', 'body_sha256')}
+            evidence.update(params=receipt.get('params'), normalized_record_index=index)
+            row = {'source_id': sid, 'id': ident, 'title': record['title'], 'published_as_reported': record['published'],
+                   'disposition': disposition, 'new_to_canonical': ident not in base, 'record': record, 'evidence': evidence}
+            raw_rows.append(row)
+            source_raw.append(row)
+            dispositions[disposition] += 1
+            if disposition in {'within_requested_source_window', 'needs_official_metadata'}:
+                eligible.append(row)
+                source_eligible.append(row)
+    today = result.get('hf_today') if result and kind == 'hf_daily' else None
+    status = 'pending' if result is None else 'partial' if result.get('error') and source_raw else 'error' if result.get('error') else 'ok'
+    if today and today.get('request_status') == 'not_ready':
+        status = 'historical_boards_ok_today_not_ready'
+    source_summaries.append({'source_id': sid, 'kind': kind, 'status': status,
+        'started_at': result['started_at'] if result else receipts[0]['requested_at'] if receipts else None,
+        'finished_at': result['finished_at'] if result else None, 'request_count': len(receipts),
+        'http_status_counts': dict(Counter(str(r.get('http_status', 'network_error')) for r in receipts)),
+        'raw_records_from_successful_responses': len(source_raw), 'raw_unique_ids': len({x['id'] for x in source_raw}),
+        'configured_window_records': len(source_eligible), 'configured_window_unique_ids': len({x['id'] for x in source_eligible}),
+        'original_collector_count': result['count'] if result else None,
+        'window_dispositions': dict(dispositions), 'error': result.get('error') if result else None,
+        'source_traversal_complete': result.get('source_traversal_complete', not bool(result.get('error'))) if result else False,
+        'hf_today': today, 'network_attempts': str(receipt_path.relative_to(ROOT))})
+
+# Only exact stable identities are coalesced here. Any approximate-title collision is held for review.
+incoming = {}
+bindings = defaultdict(list)
+for row in eligible:
+    r = deepcopy(row['record'])
+    ident = r['id']
+    bindings[ident].append(row['evidence'])
+    if ident not in incoming:
+        incoming[ident] = r
+    else:
+        for field in ['source_hits', 'seed_hits', 'code_links', 'categories', 'hf_daily_dates']:
+            incoming[ident][field] = sorted(set(incoming[ident].get(field, [])) | set(r.get(field, [])))
+        incoming[ident]['links'].update(r['links'])
+    incoming[ident]['first_seen'] = first_seen(ident, observed[ident])
+    incoming[ident]['source_observed_at'] = observed[ident]
+
+new_items, metadata_changes, provenance_updates, collisions = [], [], [], []
+for ident, record in incoming.items():
+    old = base.get(ident)
+    authority = official.get(record.get('arxiv_id'))
+    if authority:
+        fields = ['title', 'abstract', 'authors', 'published', 'updated', 'version', 'published_source',
+                  'announced', 'announced_source', 'comments']
+        if old:
+            differences = {k: {'before': old.get(k), 'official': authority.get(k)} for k in fields
+                           if old.get(k) != authority.get(k)}
+            if differences:
+                metadata_changes.append({'id': ident, 'existing_source_hash': source_hash(old),
+                    'official_arxiv_id': authority['arxiv_id'], 'differences': differences,
+                    'automatically_applied': False, 'review_required': True})
+        else:
+            for k in fields:
+                record[k] = authority[k]
+            record['links'].update(authority['links'])
+            record['metadata_pending'] = False
+            record['official_metadata_verified'] = True
+            record['official_metadata_record_id'] = authority['id']
+            if authority.get('metadata_evidence'):
+                record['official_metadata_evidence'] = authority['metadata_evidence']
+    if old:
+        updates = {k: sorted(set(record.get(k, [])) - set(old.get(k, [])))
+                   for k in ['source_hits', 'hf_daily_dates']}
+        updates = {k: v for k, v in updates.items() if v}
+        if updates:
+            provenance_updates.append({'id': ident, 'existing_source_hash': source_hash(old),
+                'existing_first_seen': old['first_seen'], 'observed_source_hash_is_not_apply_precondition': True,
+                'apply_validation': 'Check baseline first_seen then union source_hits and hf_daily_dates only; retain all science and decisions.',
+                'add_to_sets': updates, 'bindings': bindings[ident],
+                'scientific_fields_and_decisions_must_remain_unchanged': True})
+    else:
+        same = [x['id'] for x in base.values() if x['kind'] == record['kind'] and (
+            record.get('arxiv_id') and x.get('arxiv_id') == record['arxiv_id'] or
+            record['kind'] == 'paper' and similar_titles(x['title'], record['title']))]
+        if same:
+            collisions.append({'incoming_id': ident, 'possible_existing_ids': same, 'title': record['title'],
+                               'proposed_record': record, 'action': 'hold_for_identity_reconciliation'})
+        else:
+            record['intake_review_status'] = 'unreviewed_free_source_candidate'
+            new_items.append({'id': ident, 'record': record, 'bindings': bindings[ident],
+                              'formal_decision': 'defer', 'paid_stages_run': False})
+
+for item in new_items:

+assert all(incoming[k]['first_seen'] == base[k]['first_seen'] for k in incoming.keys() & base.keys())

+      "abstract": "Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. +      "abstract": "Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.",

+      "abstract": "Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively improves a target capability, operationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark, through repeated intervention, training, and evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor's aggregate score as their sole observation, so early gains give way to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau may reflect an exhausted observation rather than an exhausted capability. We introduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of harness evolution that keeps the anchor objective fixed while adapting the active observation. At a plateau, a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks; validated increments are fused back into training, while every checkpoint remains evaluated against the anchor. Across eight independently optimized anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from $66.4$ to $73.7$ under a matched data budget, outperforming FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The evolved harness further improves the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends. These results identify observation adaptation as a missing mechanism of harness evolution for sustaining post-training RSI.",

+      "abstract": "Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.",

+      "abstract": "Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \\textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.",

+      "abstract": "Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($π: \\mathcal{X} \\to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $α$-$π$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.",

+      "abstract": "Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.",

+      "abstract": "We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.",

+      "abstract": "Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.",

+      "abstract": "Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. +      "abstract": "Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.",

+      "abstract": "Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. +      "abstract": "Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.",

+      "abstract": "Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. +      "abstract": "Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost. Code and models are available at https://github.com/starsholic/AeroRSI.",

+      "abstract": "Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.",

+      "abstract": "The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. +

+## 发现与审查
+
+全部 12 路启用来源均实际尝试，原始响应和时间见 [来源整合](source-intake/README.md)、[独立核验](source-integration-crosscheck.json)及原始响应索引。11/18 HF not_ready 后继续复抓 11/17 全榜 41、11/16 全榜 40（旧快照 38，晚到 2）、11/15 空榜 0；完整成员与推荐日零漏项。3 路 arXiv 成功且本窗口为 0；5 路 RSS 的窗口数量依次为 Sakana 5、METR 6、OpenAI 47、DeepMind 7、Weco 0；GitHub 13 库均尝试，release 窗口 0。Semantic Scholar citations 窗口出现 277 次 / 246 个 ID，46 次请求中 15 次 429，180 秒截止；authors 身份查询成功但论文遍历 6 次 429，不能称完整覆盖。

+  "body": "补齐 11/16–18 的公开更新：11/16 按真实推荐日/来源窗口发布 7 篇论文（2 篇 HF、5 篇其他来源），11/17 和 11/18 发布包含真实采集、审核结果及失败边界的简报。实际审核日均为 11/18；补发说明在 HTML、Markdown 和订阅中保留。W46 收录 12 篇当周论文及 32 条历史 backlog，另列 33 篇历史回顾，不将旧论文计作今日新增。\n\n出版输入来自真实合并的 #118、#134、#135、#137、#138，逐一核验同仓分支、精确 head、CI、owner 合并、merge commit 和审核文件字节。177 次应用对应 175 个稳定 ID；两条公告的 #134 决定留在历史，当前决定来自 #135。19 项历史纳入与 10 项历史排除已落实，其余 92 项保留旧审核和逐项恢复动作。EGE 原科学审核、全部 first_seen、来源哈希及 21 份旧刊 JSON 保持；10/27 撤回和原创刊回顾保留。\n\n同时修复后续回顾被硬编码为“第 0 期 / 10 月 14–27 日”的标签，以及论文补刊 HTML 丢失出版说明的问题。新回顾展示自己的标题与审核区间；旧创刊标记保留。\n\n验证：\n\n- 本地完整测试 434 passed；补刊说明和后续回顾有针对性回归覆盖。\n- 3 份日期审核及 W46 校验通过，602 个构建产物连续生成字节一致。\n- 独立复核绑定原文/摘要、40 篇本次论文与回顾内容、W46 内容和最终渲染；全账 9,052 个稳定 ID、2,222 条 canonical 均保留可恢复状态，HF 40+41 成员/推荐日无遗漏。\n- 旧模型评测 recall 0.892857 / threshold 0.90 且评测未完成，告警保留，未降低阈值或重跑付费模型。三个手动禁用的 feed 工作流保持禁用。\n- 本轮新增付费生成请求/token 均为 0；账户余额观察减少 0.01 元，该差额不是本任务发票。\n\n以上是出版候选与检查证据。合并后仍须核验 Pages 和实际线上日报、归档、latest.json、Atom、首页与 README，才报告发布完成。\n",

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12288

General-purpose software serves many different demands, but this flexibility costs performance and efficiency on any specific demand. Software tailored to a specific demand avoids these losses, yet developing it requires substantial time and effort from human experts. AI agents offer an alternative: they can design, implement and test artefacts tailored to individual demands. We call this production paradigm Forge. Forging for a demand is economically justified when the cumulative benefit of specialisation exceeds the total cost of construction, verification and maintenance. To make Forge a repeatable production process, we propose ForgeSystem, which consists of a control layer, a forge loop and a recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop. The control layer selects which artefact serves each demand and decides which demands to forge, when to forge them and from which starting point; the forge loop iterates between production and verification until a candidate artefact passes verification; and the RSI loop draws on accumulated production records to supply starting points, refine the harness and train models. We implement ForgeSystem for training frameworks, decoding megakernels and individual computational kernels. Forged training engines reach 1.047-1.332x the model-FLOPs utilisation of their reference frameworks, forged megakernels achieve a geometric-mean decoding speedup of 1.21x over SGLang across thirteen configurations, and forged kernels match or exceed expert libraries in eighteen of twenty-two configurations, while satisfying task-specific quality requirements. Controlled comparisons show that explicit quality requirements steer agents towards optimisations that preserve training quality. We also discuss a gradual transition to Forge through service routing, and how demand-specific production may shift value accumulation and trust towards production systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18006

Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36013

General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. Specialist policies alone do not ensure task-level reliability, while powerful multimodal agents rely on costly reasoning and external experience that compact models struggle to reproduce. We introduce OmniBrain-0, a lightweight unified embodied agent that coordinates manipulation and navigation through a shared high-level decision model, integrating task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery. Our progressive training framework combines embodied pretraining, domain-specialized agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). It distills powerful teachers' interaction experience into manipulation and navigation experts, then consolidates their decision capabilities into OmniBrain-0. Unification therefore occurs within the learned decision model rather than only at the tool interface. We further introduce Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), a data flywheel in which a Meta-Agent turns execution evidence into refined rubrics, step-level reminders, and verified trajectories for domain-expert updates before their reconsolidation into OmniBrain-0 through MOPD. We evaluate OmniBrain-0 on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and R2R-CE Val-Unseen, as well as multiple real-world manipulation tasks. OmniBrain-0 combines strong cross-domain task performance with substantially lower inference and execution overhead than its closed-source teacher, demonstrating efficient transfer and consolidation of embodied capabilities into a compact unified agent.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39158

The central bottleneck in visual generation and editing has migrated from achieving pixel-level fidelity to satisfying densely constrained user specifications through increasingly agentic workflows. Prevailing agentic generation pipelines remain shallow generate-verify-rewrite loops treating VLM judgments as coarse visual feedback, either discarding repair experience or admitting ungated updates that poison skill library. With memorize and govern periods left open, they degrade into ungoverned iterators of repeated trial-and-error rather than continual self-evolving harness. Towards this issue, we present \textbf{VEvo-Harness}, the first causally-guarded continual self-evolving harness system for agentic visual generation. VEvo-Harness introduces four coupled innovations: (1) \textit{a visual traceback} that densifies sparse judgments into root-cause attributions with a hierarchical verification tree; (2) \textit{a visual continual governance} that admits only causally valid skill patches through counterfactual dual-arm image generation replay; (3) \textit{a lifecycle-managed harness state} that hierarchically distills root-cause-anchored episodes across working, experience, and pattern tiers into a persistent skill library of routable and causally verified capabilities; (4) \textit{a heterogeneous sandbox policy} that orchestrates a diverse action space of repair primitives, dynamically routing cost-aware interventions based on root causes to select the most effective strategy. VEvo-Harness surpasses state-of-the-art agentic methods and rivals proprietary generators (\textit{e.g.}, GPT-Image, Nano-Pro) while maintaining the continual harness evolution and generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39714

Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.
","createdAt":"2026-11-02T07:44:15Z","number":20,"title":"MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T02:14:54Z","url":"https://github.com/adongwanai/follow-rsi/issues/20"},{"body":"KARMA: Training-Free Knowledge-Atomic Harness Evolution for Industrial Advertising Agents

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39884

Industrial advertising agents must continually adapt their decision knowledge to changing product offerings, traffic patterns, and operating policies. We present KARMA (Knowledge-Atomic, Regression-Gated Modular Adaptation), a training-free framework that evolves six typed knowledge modules while keeping model weights and executable harness code frozen. During our evolution, a deterministic Trace Verifier maps observed errors to candidate modules, and a Critic compares successful and failed trajectories to guide a tool-constrained Evolver. The Evolver applies atomic knowledge edits, which a fixed validation gate retains only when their measured gain reaches a threshold; otherwise, the previous knowledge state is restored. We evaluate KARMA with three LLM families on cases sampled from a corpus of approximately half a million real-world operation logs across six e-commerce domains. Across 18 domain--model settings, KARMA raises the average hold-out score from 30.19 to 39.15 (+8.96 points, +29.7%). Ablations show that removing either successful or failed trajectories more than halves the average hold-out gain. Evolved knowledge also transfers across domains without further adaptation, yielding an average hold-out gain of 8.54 points across all source--target pairs. By linking retained patches to their diagnostic evidence and validation outcomes, KARMA supports inspectable, reversible knowledge adaptation for agents in Web marketplaces.
